description: How Hoover failed and Roosevelt's New Deal reshaped American government in the 1930s.
content_html:
The Wall Street Crash, 1929

On 24 October 1929 — “Black Thursday” — panic selling gripped the New York Stock Exchange. Share prices had been rising artificially throughout the 1920s, fuelled by buying on the margin. When confidence collapsed, investors raced to sell. By 29 October — “Black Tuesday” — the market had lost around 25 per cent of its value in days. Banks that had invested depositors’ money in shares now collapsed in turn, wiping out savings and triggering a chain of business failures.

Key Fact

The Wall Street Crash began on 24 October 1929 (“Black Thursday”) and worsened on 29 October (“Black Tuesday”). Within three years, around 13 million Americans were unemployed — roughly one in four workers.

Life During the Depression

By 1932, unemployment had reached approximately 25 per cent. Thousands of families lost their homes. The makeshift shanty towns that sprang up on the edges of cities became known as Hoovervilles — a bitter reference to the president many blamed for the crisis. Breadlines and soup kitchens became a feature of American cities. Farmers in the Midwest faced a double blow: banks repossessed farms while drought turned the Great Plains into a “Dust Bowl”, driving hundreds of thousands of “Okies” westward.

President Herbert Hoover was a firm believer in rugged individualism — the belief that government welfare would undermine Americans’ self-reliance. He refused to provide direct federal relief, fearing it would make people dependent on the state. His main measure, the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC, 1932), gave loans to banks and large businesses, but the benefit was slow to reach ordinary Americans.

When around 20,000 First World War veterans marched on Washington in the summer of 1932 to demand early payment of a bonus promised for 1945, Hoover sent the army to clear their camps. Images of soldiers attacking veterans destroyed what remained of his popularity. In the November 1932 election, Roosevelt won 57 per cent of the popular vote.

Roosevelt and the New Deal

Franklin D. Roosevelt took office in March 1933 with the USA in the grip of a banking crisis. His inaugural address promised action: the government would treat the Depression as a national emergency equivalent to war. Roosevelt’s approach rested on three aims — Relief, Recovery and Reform — later called the “3 Rs”.

Key Fact

Roosevelt’s New Deal had three aims: Relief (immediate help for the unemployed and poor), Recovery (restarting the economy) and Reform (changing laws to prevent another crash). These goals drove the creation of the “alphabet agencies” during the Hundred Days of legislation in 1933.

The Hundred Days and Alphabet Agencies

Between March and June 1933 — the “Hundred Days” — Roosevelt pushed an extraordinary programme through Congress. He immediately declared a four-day bank holiday to stop panic withdrawals, then used radio “fireside chats” to reassure the public. Key agencies created in this period included:

The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC, 1933) put young unemployed men to work planting trees, building roads and maintaining national parks. Over its lifetime it employed approximately 3 million men. The Agricultural Adjustment Administration (AAA, 1933) paid farmers to reduce overproduction, raising crop prices. The National Recovery Administration (NRA, 1933) set codes for fair wages, prices and working conditions in industries, though the Supreme Court struck it down in 1935 as unconstitutional.

The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA, 1933) was one of the boldest measures — a federal body that built dams and hydroelectric power stations across seven states, bringing electricity to rural areas and creating thousands of construction jobs. The Works Progress Administration (WPA, 1935), created in the Second New Deal, employed millions on public works including roads, schools and hospitals, and also funded writers, artists and musicians.

The Second New Deal, 1935

By 1935 Roosevelt faced criticism from both the left and right. Senator Huey Long argued the New Deal had not done enough for the poor; business leaders complained of excessive government interference. Roosevelt responded with the Second New Deal. The Social Security Act (1935) established unemployment insurance and old-age pensions for the first time in American history. The Wagner Act (1935) guaranteed workers’ right to join trade unions and bargain collectively.

Opposition to the New Deal

Not everyone welcomed Roosevelt’s programme. Many Republicans and business leaders argued it amounted to socialism and damaged free enterprise. The Supreme Court declared several agencies unconstitutional. Critics like Huey Long called it too conservative. When Roosevelt tried to “pack” the Supreme Court with sympathetic justices in 1937, Congress blocked him — a significant political setback. Despite these tensions, the New Deal permanently changed expectations of what the federal government should provide for citizens.
exam_tip_html: For 6-mark “Explain a Cause” questions on the Depression, identify a cause (e.g. overproduction, buying on the margin) and explain the chain of consequences rather than just describing what happened. For 16-mark period essays, you need a sustained argument and a substantiated overall judgement — don’t just list the alphabet agencies; weigh whether the New Deal achieved genuine recovery or mainly provided relief. Always use precise dates: 1929 Crash, 1933 Hundred Days, 1935 Second New Deal.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Wall Street Crash of 1929 triggered the Great Depression, with unemployment reaching around 25 per cent by 1932. Hoover’s belief in rugged individualism led him to refuse direct relief, making him deeply unpopular.
  • Roosevelt’s New Deal (from 1933) created alphabet agencies — CCC, AAA, TVA, WPA — to provide Relief, Recovery and Reform. The Hundred Days saw an unprecedented burst of legislation.
  • The Second New Deal (1935) went further, introducing the Social Security Act (pensions and unemployment insurance) and the Wagner Act (union rights), permanently expanding the federal government’s role.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Hoovervilles that appeared across the USA during the Great Depression.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names the feature (makeshift shanty towns housing homeless/unemployed Americans) AND explains one specific aspect (e.g. built from scrap materials; named sarcastically after Hoover; located on the outskirts of cities). Developing: Identifies the feature without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Roosevelt's 'Hundred Days' legislation in 1933.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Mastering: Two fully developed features, e.g. (1) It was a period of intense legislative activity March-June 1933 in which Congress passed a large number of emergency measures; (2) It produced key agencies such as the CCC and NRA designed to bring immediate relief and economic recovery. Developing: Identifies features without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Hoover's defeat in the 1932 presidential election.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. Hoover's refusal to provide direct federal relief; his handling of the Bonus Army; his belief in rugged individualism) AND explains how this cause led to electoral defeat through a developed chain of reasoning, linking public perception to the scale of unemployment and homelessness. Secure: Cause identified with some development. Developing: Simple cause stated without explanation. Emerging: Vague or asserted response.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Social Security Act of 1935.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. creation of a federal unemployment insurance scheme; introduction of old-age pensions) AND explains how this changed the relationship between citizens and the federal government, with a developed chain of reasoning. Secure: Consequence identified with some development. Developing: Simple consequence without explanation. Emerging: Vague response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) for the development of the USA in the 1930s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (jobs created, rural electrification, flood control across seven states) AND over time (model for federal intervention in the economy; lasting infrastructure; transformation of the South's economy). Secure: Addresses significance at the time with limited coverage of longer-term impact. Developing: Describes the TVA without analysing significance. Emerging: Vague or narrative only.

practice_questions.text: 'The New Deal successfully ended the Great Depression.' How far do you agree with this view? Use your knowledge of the period 1929-1939 to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs evidence on both sides and reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Should consider: evidence FOR (unemployment fell from ~25% to ~15% by 1937; alphabet agencies provided relief and infrastructure; Social Security Act created safety net) AGAINST (full recovery only came with wartime production 1941-42; 1937-38 recession when Roosevelt cut spending; Supreme Court struck down key agencies; African Americans largely excluded from benefits). Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides. Developing: Some argument, evidence limited to one side. Emerging: Narrative description without argument.

knowledge_checks.q: What name was given to the makeshift shanty towns built by homeless Americans during the Depression?
Which of the following best describes Roosevelt's three Rs?
Roosevelt's burst of emergency legislation in spring 1933 became known as the '_____'.
The _____ Act of 1935 established unemployment insurance and old-age pensions for the first time in the USA.
Match each New Deal agency to its main purpose:
right: Built dams and brought electricity to rural areas across seven states
Employed young men on conservation projects such as planting trees
Paid farmers to reduce overproduction and raise crop prices

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Wall Street Crash begin?
What were the three Rs of Roosevelt's New Deal?
flashcard_questions.a: Relief meant immediate help for the unemployed; Recovery meant restarting the economy; Reform meant changing laws to prevent another crash.

flashcard_questions.q: What was buying on the margin?
flashcard_questions.a: Buying shares with borrowed money, gambling on rising prices.
Shanty towns built by homeless Americans during the Depression, named after President Hoover.
Employed young men on conservation work such as planting trees and building roads.
Dams and hydroelectric power stations across seven states, bringing rural electrification.

flashcard_questions.q: The Hundred Days legislation ran from March to June of which year?
What two rights did the Wagner Act 1935 guarantee workers?
flashcard_questions.a: The right to join trade unions and bargain collectively.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Social Security Act 1935 introduce?
What was Hoover's belief about government welfare called?
Approximately what percentage of Americans were unemployed at the Depression's worst point?
Which veterans marched on Washington in 1932 and were dispersed by the army?
flashcard_questions.a: First World War veterans demanding early payment of a bonus.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the AAA designed to do for farmers?
flashcard_questions.a: Pay them to reduce overproduction so crop prices would rise.

glossary_terms.definition: Buying shares using borrowed money, betting prices will keep rising.
Shantytowns built by homeless Americans during the Depression, sarcastically named after President Hoover.
The idea that individuals and businesses should solve problems through hard work and self-reliance, without government handouts.
A second wave of New Deal legislation in 1935 that included the Social Security Act and the Wagner Act, extending federal support further.
